summary: FireSpot turns 25 years of satellite fire detections into one consistent record and uses it for early warning and short-term spread forecasts. MODIS (1 km, since 2000) and VIIRS (375 m, since 2012) see the same fire very differently, so splicing their archives makes detections jump x5.24 in 2012 and creates a false rising trend of +13.8 %/year. We train models on simultaneous MODIS/VIIRS observations to convert MODIS into a VIIRS-equivalent: the 2012 jump falls to x1.16 and the trend to -0.8 %/year (not significant). On top of this record, FireSpot corrects the bow-tie effect at the swath edge, flags live anomalies against a 2008-2025 same-week baseline, separates routine agricultural burning from unusual events, and forecasts spread for 1-3 days by combining machine learning with a physics simulation. Every forecast can be replayed on past fires using only data available at the start, so we report honest results, including the weak ones: about 58 % day-1 and 73-76 % day-3 accuracy within 5 km. It is a keyless, open-data research prototype with a live web app, PDF reports and CAP/GeoJSON export, built for responders, researchers and land managers.
details:
FIRESPOT: PROJECT DETAILS

One-sentence version

FireSpot turns 25 years of MODIS and VIIRS fire detections into one consistent, comparable record, uses it for live early warning, and forecasts short-term fire spread with machine learning plus a physics simulation, with every claim checked by a leak-free replay and published honestly, including the results that did not work.

1. THE PROBLEM

NASA's active-fire record is split between two instrument families that see fire very differently. MODIS (Terra since 2000, Aqua since 2002) has a pixel of about 1 km. VIIRS (Suomi NPP since 2012, NOAA-20 since 2018, NOAA-21 since 2023) has a pixel of about 375 m, so it detects smaller and cooler fires and lights up many more pixels on the same large fire. If you simply splice the two archives, detections jump x5.24 in 2012 (five countries: Brazil, Australia, India, United States, Canada), and the spliced record shows an apparent upward trend of +13.8 % per year in the detection count that is almost entirely an instrument change, not a change in fires. Anyone studying trends, comparing seasons, or building alerts on the raw splice gets misleading answers. On top of that, MODIS and VIIRS pixels grow towards the edge of the scan (the "bow-tie" effect, up to roughly 2.0 x 4.8 km), so one fire can look like several, and satellites cannot see through cloud and smoke or between passes, so "no detection" does not mean "no fire".

2. WHAT WE BUILT

FireSpot is a FastAPI backend and a no-build web application (Leaflet map, 3D globe, vanilla JavaScript, English and Polish, dark and light themes, mobile layout). It has five workspaces: Monitor (live detections), Forecast (spread forecasts), History (multi-year comparisons and the harmonized record), Alerts (regions above their seasonal norm), and Replay (honest validation on past fires). The analytics engine is a Python package ("EquiFire") with trained models shipped in the repository.

3. HOW THE HARMONIZATION WORKS (the core of the challenge)

- All detections are aggregated on a common 0.05-degree grid (about 5.5 km). One row is one satellite pass over one cell; the "cell-day" is the basic unit.

- We learn from simultaneous observations (MODIS and VIIRS over the same cell within about 30 minutes), with VIIRS as the reference.

- A size model and an FRP model (gradient-boosted regressors) convert a MODIS observation into a VIIRS-equivalent. Fire-size error is 69 % lower than raw MODIS and 24 % lower than a straight-line correction; FRP error is 18 % lower than raw MODIS.

- A reconstruction model answers the question "would VIIRS have seen fire in this cell?" for years when only MODIS existed (2000-2011). A classifier proposes candidate cells near MODIS fires and regressions estimate detection count, FRP and area. It is trained on 2012-2019, the threshold is chosen on 2020, and it is tested on 2021-2025.

- The 25-year series combines the reconstruction before 2012-01-20 with real Suomi NPP afterwards (a second VIIRS satellite is not added in the harmonized series, so the NOAA-20 start in 2018 does not create a new step).

Results on held-out years: the 2012 jump falls from x5.24 to x1.16, the apparent trend of the detection count falls from +13.8 %/yr to -0.8 %/yr (not statistically significant), total detections of the reconstruction match real VIIRS (ratio 1.00 versus 0.11 for raw MODIS), the cell overlap (IoU) rises from 0.177 to 0.248, and on the bridge years the detection ratio is 1.06 with a yearly correlation of 0.99 and FRP 1.05. Honest limits: the cell-day count still shows a x1.50 step (x1.12 after calibration to the overlap years), the reconstruction finds about 36 % of the cells VIIRS would have seen, regional totals can be biased between 0.5x and 1.5x (India, United States, Brazil), and the full 25-year record covers five countries. The cleanest measures are the detection count and FRP.

In the app: a 25-year record with raw-by-sensor and harmonized charts, a before/after slider that reveals the 2012 jump and its removal, a year-by-month activity grid (hatched where months were reconstructed from MODIS, with a rank among the same month in other years), and a map of where the reconstruction still disagrees with real VIIRS (2022-2025: reconstruction 5.0 M cell-days against 7.0 M real, recall 0.33, precision 0.46).

4. BOW-TIE CORRECTION

Scan angle is computed from the SGP4 orbit propagator and TLEs (or from the pixel size stored in FIRMS for old data). Detections from one pass are grouped with an adaptive clustering radius that depends on each pixel's footprint. At the swath edge this reduces MODIS clusters per VIIRS fire from 1.339 to 1.007 (at the cost of merging some neighbouring fires, which we state).

5. LIVE EARLY WARNING

Near-real-time FIRMS feeds are compared with an 18-year baseline of the same week (2008-2025) for each region with a z-score (levels: watch z >= 2, warning z >= 3, critical z >= 5, with an out-of-season flag). A classifier separates routine agricultural burning from unusual events using seven pieces of evidence (seasonal frequency, z-score, recurrence of the same fields year after year, one-day spike, power per detection, cluster size, persistence): 10 of 12 independent events correct (21 of 22 on the tuning set, which is optimistic). Alerts export as CAP 1.2 and GeoJSON. A separate 1 km alert model reaches 63.2 % precision on day 1 and 65.7 % over 3 days, but recall is only 9.2 % and 15.1 %. Detections are drawn coloured by age (yellow up to 3 h, orange 3-8 h, red 8-16 h, purple over 16 h), with an age filter and a time-lapse that replays the last day oldest first.

6. SPREAD FORECASTING

- Machine learning: a direct multi-horizon model (XGBoost) answers "will this cell burn within k days?" from information known at the start only, on a 41 x 41 cell window (about 225 km), with features such as distance to the front, burn history up to 365 days, sub-cell detection positions, fire size and growth, wind alignment, humidity, temperature and rain. Training uses only earlier years than the test year (walk-forward), so there is no leakage.

- Physics: Rothermel/Albini surface spread with Anderson fuel models, Simard fuel moisture, an elliptical front and crown-fire initiation for forests, solved as a minimum-travel-time raster at 250 m, driven by gridded hourly weather (Open-Meteo), ESA WorldCover fuel, Copernicus DEM slope, OpenStreetMap barriers (roads, rivers, built-up) and Sentinel-2 dryness, optionally calibrated to the fire's recent growth.

- Blend: a small model combines the ML probability with physics features.

Measured on unseen fires (100 fires per year, within 5 km): day 1 about 57-59 %, day 3 about 73-76 %; strict same-cell overlap on day 3 about 25-31 %. We did NOT reach the 70 % day-1 target, and the ML + physics blend did not beat ML alone (differences within noise). The physics simulator alone was checked on 20 fires and is offered as a scenario tool, not an accurate predictor.

- Replay: a leak-free mode forecasts a past fire using a copy of the fire index with the entire future removed, then reveals what happened (hits, misses, false alarms, strict and within 5 km, with an observation mask for cells the satellite could not see). On six saved incidents, 3-day results within 5 km range from 0.71 to 0.93; day 1 exceeds 0.70 in only two of six.

- Speed: the full ML + physics result takes a median of 5.5 s on saved incidents and 13.7 s on fresh areas (warm disk caches); a brand-new place with no cached landscape can take 2-3 minutes.

7. ADD-ON MODULES

Next-pass countdown (SGP4 for five satellites), blind spots (cloud visibility), weather scenarios (hypothetical), exposure of OpenStreetMap assets over time (not damage, no monetary values), incident brief and per-view PDF export, drone reconnaissance route (GPX, KML, Litchi CSV, GeoJSON; larger standoff on the downwind side; flight-time budget; planning aid only), CO2 and carbon-value ticker (Wooster 0.368 kg/MJ, biome emission factors, an assumed carbon price), Direct Broadcast station geometry (orbit geometry only; we have no X-band receiver), sun-satellite geometry (sun-glint risk), detection latency measured by our own poller, scope flag (is this case similar to what the model was trained on), independent burned area from EFFIS (Europe only), Monte Carlo ensemble frequency (not a probability), nowcasting of the next observation, a firebreak what-if sandbox (heuristic score), priority ranking, rule-based explanations, an optional Telegram alert (user's own bot token), and a temporary share link. The weaker or experimental ones sit in a collapsed "Laboratory" group so that the main interface stays focused.

8. NASA AND OTHER DATA

NASA FIRMS (MODIS, VIIRS Suomi NPP, NOAA-20, NOAA-21; archive per-country CSVs and near-real-time feeds). All sources are free and need no API key or account: Open-Meteo, ESA WorldCover, Copernicus DEM, OpenStreetMap (Overpass), Sentinel-2 (Earth Search), CelesTrak, NOAA GOES (AWS), RainViewer, Meta/CIESIN HRSL, EFFIS.

9. TOOLS, LANGUAGES, HARDWARE

Python 3.11+, FastAPI, XGBoost (CUDA optional), NumPy, pandas, SciPy, shapely, SGP4/Skyfield, Playwright (PDF), Leaflet, globe.gl, vanilla JavaScript and CSS (no build step), memory-mapped Parquet/NumPy indexes. It runs on an ordinary laptop (a 76 MB spread model, about 150 MB of pre-trained models; an optional NVIDIA GPU speeds training). Served through a tunnel; 76 API operations; 286 backend tests plus 22 unit tests pass.

10. WHAT MAKES IT CREATIVE

We treated "less but better" as a design rule: one honest chain from instrument physics to a decision aid. Harmonization, bow-tie correction, anomaly logic, spread physics and replay validation are connected in one product instead of separate demos. We publish negative results (geostationary GOES adds only +2.5 percentage points of coverage, an explosive-growth classifier reaches an AUC of 0.68 with 17 % precision, the MIR/TIR sub-pixel fire area changes by a factor of about 26 with the assumed fire temperature, calibration did not significantly improve the Brier score), correct our own numbers when we find mistakes, and label every estimate as an estimate.

11. FACTORS THE TEAM CONSIDERED

Data leakage (walk-forward and replay with the future removed), what satellites cannot see (cloud, smoke, passes, scan angle), instrument differences, uncertainty and calibration, who the users are (responders, researchers, land managers, insurers), responsible use (not for evacuation or dispatch decisions; no monetary damage claims; carbon price is an assumption), accessibility (keyboard use, text size, contrast, reduced motion), a mobile layout, reproducibility (one command downloads the data, every figure is tied to a report file), and openness (keyless data, open code, licence-checked sources).

12. IMPACT

Researchers get a comparable 25-year fire record and a documented method for combining MODIS and VIIRS. Responders and land managers get explained early warnings, a view of what the satellites could and could not see, and short-term spread estimates with their limits. The method, models, data pipeline, a 100-page guide and all reports are open for others to reuse and improve.

13. HONEST LIMITATIONS

Ground truth is VIIRS detections, which miss fires under cloud and smoke. Forecasts are uncalibrated; day-1 accuracy is below the target; the physics simulator is validated on only 20 fires and backtests use observed rather than forecast weather. The 25-year record and the alert baseline fully cover five countries. Several experimental modules have weak validation and are labelled as such. This is a research prototype and must not be used for operational decisions.
